It's actually pretty easy.

The USA has so many countries who hold debt in USD that they can cause a very short period of ridiculous inflation to pay all the debts off.

Then because the USA has the largest military in the world, they either start a new currency or revalue the dollar on the end of a gun.

There is actually nothing to see here.

Isn't it impossible to pay back the debt?

Here's the scenario:

The central bank (Fed, EZB, etc.) can create money out of nothing, they just print it.

To get it into circulation, someone needs to take a loan from the central bank.

Say, we have two parties (A and B), and both take a 100$ loan from the central bank (C), with 10% interest. Let's say this is a one-time interest payment to keep things simple.

A: 100$ funds, 110$ debt

B: 100$ funds, 110$ debt

C: 0$ funds

Now, in order for A to pay back his debt, he needs to sell something or provide a service to B. Let's say, A makes 10$ from B:

A: 110$ funds, 110$ debt

B: 90$ funds, 110$ debt

C: 0$ funds

Now A can pay back the loan to the central bank. The loaned money gets destroyed (since it was created out of nothing):

A: 0$ funds, 0$ debt

B: 90$ funds, 110$ debt

C: 10$ funds

Usually the profit the central bank makes gets transferred to the state. Let's be charitable and say that B provides a service for the government, so the 10$ go to B.

A: 0$ funds, 0$ debt

B: 100$ funds, 110$ debt

C: 0$ funds

As you can clearly see, B now has 10$ that he can't possibly pay back, ever, since the money he needs to pay back those 10$ does not exist in the economy. The only way to pay the debt is for anybody to take out another loan:

A: 100$ funds, 110$ debt

B: 100$ funds, 110$ debt

C: 0$ funds

So we're right back at the beginning. There's no way you can ever pay the debt, since every time anybody takes out a loan to pay the debt, it simply creates new debt somewhere else in the system. This is all without compound interest. If you add compound interest you have debt that increases without the money supply increasing. So in actuality we're looking more at something like this:

A: 100$ funds, 111$ debt <- added 1$ compound interest

B: 100$ funds, 111$ debt <- here too of course

C: 0$ funds

A renders services to B:

A: 111$ funds, 111$ debt

B: 89$ funds, 111$ debt

C: 0$ funds

A pays pack loan:

A: 0$ funds, 0$ debt

B: 89$ funds, 111$ debt

C: 11$ funds

C transfers profits to B (via the government):

A: 0$ funds, 0$ debt

B: 100$ funds, 111$ debt

C: 0$ funds

A takes out loan again:

A: 100$ funds, 110$ debt

B: 100$ funds, 111$ debt <- 1$ compound interest is still there

C: 0$ funds

Since there's no way to decrease the total amount of debt, and compound interest increases the total amount of debt in the system constantly, there's only one conclusion: the debt can only ever increase, the faster the more money is in circulation.

The only way I can think of to ever decrease the debt is for the clients of the central bank (countries and regular banks) to go bankrupt. And we've seen a string of bail-outs of those entities lately ... I wonder why.
